9.25

F. Simple Past III: Strong verbs

Now the real fun begins.

While the vast majority of verbs in German are weak verbs with predictable Simple Past forms, the most commonly used verbs in German — and English, for that matter — happen to be strong verbs. Strong verbs in German change their stems (think of English: do → did; write → wrote; eat → ate), which means that learning the forms requires frequent use and review.


F.1

Review: sein

The most commonly used strong verb is, of course, sein — for which you’ve already learned the Simple Past tense forms:


singular

plural

first-person

ich war

wir waren

second-person

du warst (familiar)

Sie waren (formal)

ihr wart (familiar)

Sie waren (formal)

third-person

er/der Mann war

sie/die Frau war

es/das Kind war

sie/die Leute waren

Several important features of strong verbs in the Simple Past can be seen here:

  • The stem undergoes a change from the infinitive form: sein → war.

  • The conjugations for ich and er / sie / es are identical: just the modified stem, with no ending.

  • The conjugations for du / Sie / wir / ihr / sie (pl.) are formed by adding their respective endings to the modified stem: -st / -en / -en / -t / -en.

From 1934 to 1937 the graphic artist Erich Ohser created a series of wordless cartoons in the Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung — 137 episodes all together — under the title Vater und Sohn. The disarming simplicity and charm of these stories belie another facet of Ohser’s work, namely, the political cartoons he drew (and published under pseudonyms) that skewered Joseph Goebbels and Adolf Hitler. These quickly led to a publishing ban on Ohser’s work, and, when the pseudonyms no longer protected his identity, to his arrest and imprisonment.

G. Past Perfect tense


G.1.

When narrating a series of events, you sometimes need to emphasize that one event (A) comes before another (B). This might be the case, for example, if you happen to mention (B) first, and then need to clarify that (A) came before that; or if (B) only makes sense if (A) happened first:

There were no more umbrellas at beach, since the other tourists had already taken them all.

When you read (or hear) had already taken, you mentally place that action before the discovery that there were no more umbrellas, because of the verb had taken, as well as the adverbial element already.

The verb had taken is in the Past Perfect tense. English speakers don’t use the Past Perfect very often in conversation, and neither do Germans. In most situations, the sequence of (A) and (B) is clear simply because (A) is mentioned first, followed by (B).

But where more precision is needed, both German and English make use of the Past Perfect tense to establish the correct sequence of events:

Es gab keine Sonnenschirme mehr, denn die anderen Touristen hatten sie alle schon genommen.

There were no more umbrellas, since the other tourists had already taken them all.

Wir waren nur zu dritt da, denn Jonas war nicht rechtzeitig aufgestanden.

There were only three of us there, since Jonas had not gotten up on time.
G.1
label: G.1

content:
G.2.

As you can see, and as you may have noticed in several of the Interaktionen in this section, the Past Perfect tense closely parallels the structure of the Perfect tense. It consists of an auxiliary verb in V1 position — either haben or sein, depending on the main verb — and the past participle of that verb at the end of the clause (V2). The critical difference is that the auxiliary verbs are the Simple Past forms of haben and sein: hatte and war.

nehmen: hatte … genommen had taken

aufstehen: war … aufgestanden had gotten up

[NB: English does the same thing, using had instead of have in forming the Past Perfect: had taken / had gotten up.]
